name: Grace Hansen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm a senior field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We have no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government, and we don't sell anything or campaign for any side. Your answers are confidential. What happens on an ordinary shift?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I start the water truck before the haul convoy, check its tyres and spray the dust down on the road to the pit. I'm 58 and fairly new to mining, so I still ask for help when a pump sounds wrong. The pay is unusually good for me, and my partner Elise and I have saved more than six months of bills; our children are grown. I finished secondary school and learned this vehicle on the job. What I like is seeing a clean road behind me, though I don't like holding up a whole line of trucks when I need a second try at a turn.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the morning crew that a little office automation won't stop the dust rising on our haul road. I might use a phone tool now and then to check a maintenance term, but I'd still ask a mechanic before touching the pump.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think my place depends on proving I can do the job, because I'm still one of the junior drivers. Our savings make a quiet month possible, but Elise's part-time bookshop wage won't replace mine if the mine cuts shifts for ordinary business reasons.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the water-truck rounds and practise the tight turn by the east ramp with my trainer this month. I'd put the next overtime payment into the house fund, since our children have their own expenses now and no longer need school money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel fairly settled about AI in this picture. I still feel a small knot when I slow a convoy, because the crew can see I haven't been driving here for years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens when that turn goes wrong?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The truck has a long tail and I once stopped too far across the lane. My trainer waved the haul convoy around and had me try again after lunch. Nobody shouted, but I don't want to make that a habit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What is the house fund for?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our kitchen window lets rain in around the frame. We can pay to replace it, though I'd rather do it without dipping into the main savings. The children are grown and pay their own bills, so overtime can go there.

say: I'd say **dust control** still needs a driver who can see the road and the trucks behind her.
I might use a **phone tool** for a maintenance term, but I'd check any repair with a mechanic.
think: My **junior place** is a more immediate risk than small AI changes at the mine.
Our **savings** help, but Elise's bookshop pay could not replace my higher mine wage.
do: Practise the **east-ramp turn** with my trainer while keeping the water-truck rounds.
Put the next **overtime payment** into our house fund.
feel: **Fairly settled** about AI, with a small worry about being seen learning on the job.
S0.quote: Our savings make a quiet month possible, but Elise's part-time bookshop wage won't replace mine if the mine cuts shifts for ordinary business reasons.
fieldNote: Grace treats **driver skill** and mine business conditions as more immediate than the card's modest AI change.
The **strong cushion** eases her worry, while her partner's smaller wage makes keeping mine income important to the household.

steps.text: Continue water-truck rounds and practise the east-ramp turn
Add the next overtime payment to the house fund

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the office will feel this sooner than the pit, because software can plan deliveries and check paperwork. I would ask for the new route display to be tested on a real dusty shift before anyone says it saves drivers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I use AI occasionally, so I'm not afraid of every screen, but the mine's route choices can put me in a blind bend. I might be the junior person asked to follow a system that an experienced driver would challenge. That makes me watchful.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd sit with the dispatcher for one afternoon if they introduce an automated route display. I'd compare its proposed runs with my handwritten dust notes for the east road before accepting it as reliable.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm interested in whether the display helps us. I'm also uneasy about a machine route being treated as an answer when I can see the road is unsafe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What is in those dust notes?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I write down which stretches go pale first, the wind direction and where water pools. Last Friday the east road dried before the yard did, although the chart said the opposite. A route plan has to notice wind and water on the east road.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you refuse a route that looked wrong?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop and call the dispatcher, then explain the bend and the truck traffic. I wouldn't simply ignore the screen; I'd need the change logged so the next driver understands it too. A good system should let us correct it.

say: I'd say **dispatch and paperwork** change first, while dusty roads still need drivers.
I'd ask for a **real-shift trial** of any route display before management counts the time saved.
think: I could use a **new screen**, but a junior driver may be pushed to obey it despite a blind bend.
I worry about **unsafe routes** being defended because a system chose them.
do: Sit with the **dispatcher** for an afternoon if an automated display is introduced.
Compare the display's **east-road runs** with my handwritten dust notes.
feel: **Interested**, and uneasy if a screen's plan outranks what drivers can see.
S1.quote: I might be the junior person asked to follow a system that an experienced driver would challenge.
fieldNote: Grace's occasional **AI use** makes her willing to test a display, but she wants evidence from actual driving conditions.
She worries that **junior standing** could make it harder for her to contest an unsafe software route.

steps.text: Learn the new route display beside the dispatcher if introduced
Compare automated east-road routes with handwritten dust notes

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my crew that AGI in 2028 could replace a lot of the mine's planning and checking, even though our trucks still need drivers then. Robot trucks around 2031 are the point when I would ask whether my own post survives.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be 60 for the thinking change and about 63 when robots arrive. The water truck might be harder to automate than a haul truck, but I don't know enough to count on that. My savings could bridge a gap; they are not a retirement income.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the supervisor now which mine vehicles still need drivers after the first robot trials. If the water-truck shifts are cut in 2031, I'd apply for another local mine's safety vehicle vacancy before giving up paid work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel alarm rising when I imagine losing the wage this soon after learning the machine. Having a few months of savings lets me make calls instead of freezing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why a safety vehicle?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I already watch traffic, visibility and water on the roads. That doesn't make me a safety officer, but another mine has drivers who carry the inspection crew between sites. I'd apply for that vehicle role and be clear about what I can do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Elise that night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell her the date I heard and which jobs I could apply for. She'd likely ask me to keep the bookshop shifts out of the calculation unless her hours are guaranteed. We'd open the savings sheet together, not just hope the mine changes its mind.

say: I'd say **AGI in 2028** changes mine planning before robot trucks threaten drivers around 2031.
I'd ask management what happens to **water-truck posts** during robot trials.
think: At **63**, I could lose a job I have only recently learned.
Our **savings** bridge a gap, but they do not tell me how to afford retirement.
do: Ask the **supervisor** which vehicles will still need drivers after robot trials.
Apply for a **safety-vehicle vacancy** at another local mine if water-truck shifts are cut.
feel: **Anxious** about the wage, with enough savings to make a few practical calls.
S2.quote: My savings could bridge a gap; they are not a retirement income.
fieldNote: She separates **2028 planning automation** from robot work around 2031, when her own driving wage may be cut.
Several nearby mines offer **possible vacancies**, but she does not assume her water-truck experience guarantees a transfer.

steps.text: Ask the supervisor which vehicles retain drivers after robot trials
Apply for a local safety-vehicle vacancy if water-truck shifts fall

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the crew AGI in 2031 gives us five years to see the office changes before robot vehicles arrive around 2034. I would ask for proper training places rather than a vague promise that drivers can move somewhere else.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At 63 when AGI arrives, I may still need mine pay, and by the robot date I'd be about 66. Five years is enough to test another skill if the training is real. I don't want to spend our savings on a course with no recognised job at the end.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd apply next year for the mine's paid road-safety course if it opens to drivers. I'd keep my water-truck shifts while I learn and check what a safety driver earns at the other mines before choosing a move.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel more able to plan than in the fast case. I'm still concerned about the pay cut that might come with a different job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make the course useful?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It would have to teach inspections in the pit, radio calls and how to stop traffic safely. I know the road from the water truck, but I don't know the full safety job. I'd want someone who hires for it to recognise the course.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you take lower pay to leave the truck?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Some reduction might be possible after we calculate our bills. Elise and I have savings, but the roof and health costs don't announce themselves politely. I'd compare actual offers, not make a brave statement at the lunch table.

say: I'd say **2031 AGI** allows time to observe office changes before robot vehicles around 2034.
I'd ask for **named training places**, not an undefined promise of transfer.
think: At **66** when robots arrive, I might still rely on the mine wage.
I'd risk training time if a **recognised job** followed, but not our savings for an uncertain course.
do: Apply for the mine's **paid road-safety course** next year if driver places open.
Keep driving the **water truck** while comparing local safety-driver wages.
feel: **More capable** of planning, though a lower wage after transfer still worries me.
S3.quote: I don't want to spend our savings on a course with no recognised job at the end.
fieldNote: She would use the warning for **paid road-safety training**, but only if the mine opens places to current drivers.
Her concern remains **household income**: a safer role with much lower pay might not solve the problem.

steps.text: Apply for a paid mine road-safety course if driver places open
Continue water-truck shifts while comparing local safety-driver pay

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say AGI in 2036 is far enough away for the mine to show what changes actually work; robots around 2039 are the driving question. I'd encourage the younger crew to ask for job figures year by year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be 68 when AGI comes and about 71 at the robot date. I might retire before then, but I won't assume the numbers work without checking them. Elise may also choose to reduce her bookshop hours, which changes our calculation.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd sit down with Elise every spring to compare savings, mine pay and likely household costs. I'd keep taking shifts while my health allows. I would decide when to leave the mine from our household figures, not an AI date.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel calmer having a decade to make decisions. There's still uncertainty about our future costs, but it doesn't press on me this week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why would you ask about younger drivers' jobs?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My own working years may be nearly done by then, but the driver who trained me has a child just starting school. A year's warning would be little use to that family. I want numbers early enough for people to learn something else.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you stop driving?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pain, a safer job that pays enough or figures showing we can afford to stop. I enjoy the mine, but I wouldn't keep driving simply to prove a point. Elise and I would choose together.

say: I'd say **2036 AGI** gives the mine time to show evidence, with robot driving around 2039.
I'd ask for **yearly job figures** so younger drivers can plan their working lives.
think: I would be **68** for AGI and about 71 for hands-on robots.
I may retire first, but **Elise's hours** and our future costs still need checking.
do: Review **savings and bills** with Elise each spring before setting a leaving date.
Keep the **water-truck shifts** while health and the household figures allow.
feel: **Calmer** with time to choose, despite uncertainty about later household costs.
S4.quote: I would decide when to leave the mine from our household figures, not an AI date.
fieldNote: The decade lets Grace make **yearly household reviews** instead of treating retirement as automatic at a particular age.
She brings **younger drivers** into the discussion because their paid working years extend beyond the robot date.

steps.text: Review savings and household bills with Elise each spring
Continue paid water-truck shifts while health and finances allow

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 troubles me most because the robot date would come when I'm around 63 and still likely counting on the mine wage. A real paid road-safety place, with a recognised route to work, would help me. My savings could bridge a gap; they are not a retirement income.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask what happens to drivers who are still learners when the company offers retraining. I can move into a new subject, but I need the instruction to start where I actually am. A glossy course meant for experienced mechanics would not do me much good.

headlineQuote: A route plan has to notice wind and water on the east road.
portrait: Grace is a **58-year-old** junior water-truck driver, still improving difficult turns at a large mine.
She and her partner Elise have **strong savings** and grown children, yet the higher mine wage remains important.
She uses **AI occasionally** and tests new displays against real road conditions before trusting them.
She seeks **paid road-safety training** in the faster cases and checks retirement figures with Elise in the longer one.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** worries her most because robot vehicles around 2031 could end her wage at about age 63.
whatWouldHelp: A **paid road-safety place** recognised by local mines would help her move without spending the household savings.
